units.text: You wake up in your own room, in the middle of the night, because something close to your bed has made a sound.
You open your eyes and you see only black.
You lie still and you listen.
Then your eyes begin to work in the dark, and you understand that the black above you is not the ceiling.
It is two empty holes, in a face with no eyes, leaning over you, close enough to touch.
Something dark is running out of those holes and down the side of its face.
This is the story of the thing people call Eyeless Jack.
Let us go back to the beginning.
My name is Mitch, and until a few years ago I did not believe in anything I could not touch.
I lost my house that spring.
The bank took it, the way banks do, slowly and then all at once.
My older brother Edwin called me the same week and told me to stop being proud and come and live with him.
We had not seen each other properly in ten years, so part of me was actually glad about it.
His house was one of those cheap places at the end of a long street, with a wooden porch, a bare back yard, and pine woods standing behind the fence.
It took me a week to unpack.
Boxes in the hall, boxes on the landing, boxes down the side of the bed.
"Take the back room. It is quiet, and the window gets the morning."
The back room was quiet.
That is the part I think about now.
I slept well that first week.
I remember thinking that this was the first time in a year that I had felt safe.
About a week in, I woke up at one in the morning.
There was a sound coming from outside, under the window.
A slow, careful rustling, the way something moves when it does not want to be heard.
I lay there and listened to it for a long time.
I told myself it was a raccoon in the bins.
We had raccoons.
Everybody on that street had raccoons.
So I turned over and I went back to sleep.
In the morning I told Edwin about it over his coffee.
"Raccoons. They get into everything out here. I will put a brick on the bin lid."
He put a brick on the bin lid, and we both forgot about it.
I want you to notice how easy that was.
A noise outside, a simple answer, and a man can sleep for one more night.
The next night was different.
I did not wake up slowly.
I came awake all at once, the way you do when a sound belongs inside your room and not outside it.
I was almost sure I had heard my window being lifted open.
And then a thump, soft and heavy, like a person landing on the floor with their knees bent.
I sat straight up and I looked at every corner of that room.
The window was shut.
The boxes were where I had left them.
Nothing moved.
I listened until my ears were ringing with the effort, and the house gave me nothing back.
After a while I told myself I had been dreaming, and I lay down again with my back to the wall.
I slept.
That is the thing I cannot explain to anybody who has not been through it.
I slept.
The next morning I walked into the kitchen, and Edwin dropped his cup.
It hit the floor and broke and he did not even look at it.
He was looking at my face.
"Mitch. Do not touch it. Just stand there."
He took the little mirror off the shelf by the door and held it up in front of me.
There was a long cut down my left cheek.
Clean, straight, and nothing like a scratch from a nail or a corner of a box.
I had not felt it.
I had slept through the whole night and I had not felt a thing.
Edwin drove me to the hospital with both hands tight on the wheel and the radio off.
The doctor cleaned the cut and asked me the questions they ask.
"Do you drink before bed? Do you take anything to sleep? Has anyone in your family ever walked in their sleep?"
I said no to all of it, and he wrote it down anyway.
"The most likely answer is that you did this to yourself while you were asleep. It happens more than people think."
I was ready to believe him.
I wanted to believe him.
A sleepwalking man is a problem you can fix.
Then he stopped writing, and his face changed, and he asked me to lie back and lift my shirt.
He did not say anything for a long moment.
"Mitch. There is a surgical cut in your side, and it has been closed again with stitches. Neat ones."
He turned the screen of the scanner round so that I could see it myself.
I am not a doctor and even I could see that there was a space where something should have been.
"You have lost your left kidney. Some time last night. I am sorry. We do not know how."
I remember the sound of the clock on that wall.
I remember a trolley going past the door.
I remember the word last night, sitting in the middle of the room like a stone.
Somebody had opened me up while I slept, taken a piece of me out, closed me again, and gone back out through the window.
This story is my own retelling of the creepypasta Eyeless Jack, first posted by a user called Azelf5000.
They kept me in for the day and sent me home with painkillers and a sheet of paper about infection.
Edwin wanted me to sleep on the couch, downstairs, near him.
I said I would be fine in the back room.
I was not being brave.
I think I wanted to know.
I lay in that bed with the lamp off and the painkillers moving in my blood, and at some point I fell asleep.
Around midnight I opened my eyes, and it was there.
It was standing over my bed, bent forward at the waist, close enough that I could feel the air move when it breathed.
A black hooded top, the hood up.
A face the colour of old grey paint, with no nose and no mouth at all.
And where the eyes should have been there were two black holes that went back further than a face should go.
Something dark was running slowly out of both of them, down what would have been its cheeks, and dripping on to my blanket.
I did not scream.
I want to be honest about that, because people always ask.
I did not make a sound.
My hand went sideways, on its own, to the little shelf by the bed where I kept my camera.
I lifted it, and I took the picture.
The flash filled that room for half a second, and in that half a second I saw all of it at once, every fold of the hood and every finger.
Then the dark came back, and it came at me.
It was fast, and it was strong, and it went for my chest with both hands.
I got my foot up between us and I kicked it in the face as hard as a man with stitches can kick anything.
It went backwards into the boxes and I was out of that bed and through the door.
I grabbed my wallet off the hall table.
I do not know why.
You do strange things.
I went out of the front door in bare feet and I ran down that long street with the porch lights going past me.
I did not shout for Edwin.
I did not go back for him.
I have had a long time to think about that.
At the end of the street I went over the fence and into the pine woods behind the houses.
There was no moon under those trees.
There was no path either, and I was running on roots and stones.
I remember the cold, and my own breath, and the stitches in my side pulling with every step.
I remember looking back once and seeing nothing at all, which was somehow worse.
Then my foot caught a rock and the ground came up and hit me, and the woods went out like a light.
I woke up in a hospital bed with a drip in my arm and daylight on the wall.
It was the same doctor.
He came in with my notes under his arm and he sat down, which nobody does when the news is good.
"There is good news and bad news, Mitch."
"The good news is that you were lucky. Cuts, bruises, a mild concussion. Your parents are on their way to collect you."
I let out a breath I think I had been holding since midnight.
"The bad news is that your brother was found in the house this morning. He was killed. I am very sorry."
"Killed by what?"
He looked at the floor, and then he looked at me, and he told me the truth, which was that nobody could say.
I had kicked it in the face and run out of the house, and it had not followed me into those woods.
It had not needed to.
There was already somebody in that house.
Three days later my parents drove me back to get my things.
They waited in the car.
My mother did not want to go in and my father did not want to leave her out there on her own.
The porch light was still on in the middle of the day.
Edwin always forgot it.
I went up the stairs to the back room and I made myself calm, the way you do when you have practised being calm in the car.
My camera was still on the shelf where my hand had left it.
I put it in my pocket.
And then I stopped, because I could see along the hallway from there, and the hallway was not empty.
I am not going to describe what the police had already photographed in that house.
My brother was at the far end of it, and that is all I will say.
There was something small lying on the floor beside him, wrapped in a piece of cloth.
I picked it up without thinking, the way you pick up anything that does not belong on a floor.
I carried it out past my mother and my father and I sat down in the back seat of their car with it in my lap.
We were two streets away before I opened the cloth.
It was the piece of me that had been taken out of my side four nights before.
Some of it was gone.
There was a dark stain on the cloth around it, the same colour as the stuff that had been running out of those empty holes.
I was sick in my mother's car, and then I cried, and my father did not stop driving.
The picture is still on that camera.
I have never shown it to anybody who did not ask twice.
It is dark, and it is blurred, because my hand was shaking.
But the hood is there, and the face is there, and the two holes are there.
And there is one more thing in that photograph that I have never been able to explain.
The thing is not looking at me.
It is looking past my shoulder, at the door of my room, which I had left open, and which leads to the rest of that house.
Would you have taken the photograph?
